title: None of it is yours
hookLine: wealth, spouse, property: you call them yours, but none goes with you (Salok M9, ang 1426)

cards: Clearing out a parent's house after they've died is a strange job. Every drawer is full of things that mattered to someone. The good china saved for guests who rarely came.
A box of receipts from 1987. A coat that still smells like them. Each object was mine to someone for decades.
Now it's a question: keep, give, throw away. And the one who called it all mine isn't here to decide. Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifth salok stands in exactly that room.

teach.b: The salok begins dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan. In paraphrase: wealth, spouse, all your property, all the things you take to be your own: not one of them is your companion. Says Nanak, know this as true.
Dhan is wealth. Sampat is property. Daaraa is wife, or spouse.

teach.h: APUNEE KAR MAAN: CALLING IT MINE.
teach.b: And the key phrase is apunee kar maan: to treat as one's own. That's what the salok is really looking at: not the things, but the word mine stamped on them. Listing a spouse beside the money can sound harsh.
But the Sikh path is lived in families; the ninth Guru himself was a husband and father. The salok isn't saying don't love your husband or wife.
It's saying that even the person closest to you isn't a possession, and doesn't travel with you through death. Heard that way, it's almost tender.
The people we love were never ours to own. They were gifts, given for a while. And notice the word companion, sangee.
The salok isn't asking you to throw anything away. It's asking: who walks with you all the way?
On day five hundred twelve, Sukhmani said the earned Name and the self your deeds shaped are what go along.

This couplet makes the same point from the other side, by naming what stays behind. The result is a lighter grip. You can enjoy a good house, love a family, earn honestly, and still say quietly: this is lent to me.

how: The Sikh path is a householder's path of work, owning and sharing; the ninth Guru's salok on wealth, spouse and property is heard among his saloks at the bhog of a complete reading, including readings held after a death, as a reminder that nothing we own goes with us.

o: wealth saved up for later years
a companion who walks with you
mine, what we claim as our own

games.q: none of it is yours — tap the pairs.

s: the salok tells Sikhs not to marry or own anything
the Sikh path is a householder's path; it loosens the word mine, not love or work.
the salok says none of these is your companion all the way
wealth, spouse, property: none goes with you.
the salok's real target is the word mine
apunee kar maan: treating things and people as one's own.

games.q: the salok names wealth, spouse and property. what does it say about them?
o: they are evil and should be given up.
none of them is your companion all the way.
they come with you if you earn them honestly.
games.why: dhan daaraa sampat sagal, jin apunee kar maan: none of these is a companion. says Nanak, know this as true.

practice: Pick up something you own and care about, a ring, a watch, a mug, your phone, and hold it in an open hand, feeling its weight and thinking about where it came from.

Say quietly to yourself, this is lent to me, and notice whether the grip tightens or loosens; then put it down gently and sit with empty hands. If you pray, you can give thanks to Waheguru for what's been lent.

wordCard.voice: Meraa, mine. The fifth salok loosens the grip of this word: wealth, spouse and property, everything we call meraa, is not our companion all the way; know this as true.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: meraa, mine. The salok loosens the grip of this little word.

carryVoice: Your line: none of it goes. Mine gets quieter when you hear it as lent. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, salok 5 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1426)
Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 19 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 288)
